title: Dendritic Forest Management (HDFM framework)
description:
Working paper, not peer reviewed; all results are from synthetic landscapes and none is field-validated.

Open-source landscape planning around roads and waterways: reproducible geometric assessments, a self-hosted web workspace and experimental Hierarchical Dendritic Forest Management research tools.

Correction in v0.6.0. This version corrects the network-topology results of v0.5.0. That version reported local choice entropy of 2.28 ± 0.04 nats for minimum spanning trees and +21.5% to +37.3% for alternative networks. Those values were not produced by the linked code and cannot hold for 15-patch networks under the paper's own definition, which caps a tree at 0.62 nats. Recomputed from the code at tag v0.6.0 (hdfm-framework/examples/reproduce_topology_table.py, seeds 42 to 141), minimum spanning trees average 0.423 ± 0.004 nats, against 0.490 to 1.023 nats for relative neighbourhood (+15.9%), Gabriel (+68.3%), k-nearest-neighbour (+131.9%) and Delaunay (+141.7%) networks. The difference mainly reflects the smaller number of corridors per patch in a tree; the minimum spanning tree is not the lowest-entropy tree (a star network beats it in all 100 landscapes). Adding loops costs +28% to +137% extra corridor area, not +1.8% to +5.1% as Table 3 stated.

The cost model is withdrawn pending correction: 14,000 ha at $2,000/ha/yr is about $28 million a year, not the $2.8 million stated, and the corrected figure reverses the cost comparison. The Table 2 critical widths do not follow from the paper's formula (which gives 74, 138, 163 and 245 m) and cite no calibration studies. Figures 2 to 4, the failure-probability results and the backwards-optimization results have no reproducing script yet and should not be cited. The full list is in the erratum.
notes: Status: software pilot and working research, not peer reviewed and not field-validated. The geometric screening tools do not establish ecological viability, regulatory compliance or an optimal plan. AI use: much of the code and documentation was written with AI coding assistants (mainly Claude by Anthropic, some OpenAI Codex); Justin D. Hart reviews the changes and is the accountable author. No AI tool is listed as an author.
